Period schedule:

Total: 10 periods · 7h 30min

periods.activity_title: Mean as a Balance Point: Building the Geometric Picture

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: A dot plot shows a collection with its mean of 9 but one dot is missing; mark the missing value to restore the balance.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Three dot plots show song lengths for different albums; identify which has a mean of 5.57 minutes and explain the reasoning.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: where is the 'fair centre' of a set of numbers? Students place three numbers on a hand-drawn number line and physically mark where they feel balance lies, then share reasoning with a partner.

Introduce the balance-point model from section 5.1 prose: the mean is the unique point where total distance to the left equals total distance to the right. Students verify with two- and three-number collections on their own number lines, then argue in pairs why shifting the point disturbs the equality of distances.

Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.113 ("A dot plot shows a collection with its mean of 9 but one dot is missing; mark the missing value to restore the balance.") — students use the distance-balance argument to locate the missing dot, then articulate why their choice is the only one that works.

Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.114 ("Three dot plots show song lengths for different albums; identify which has a mean of 5.57 minutes....") — groups nominate the correct dot plot and explain using the balance-point reasoning developed above; class reaches a shared justification.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse the balance point with the midrange (average of the smallest and largest values); draw attention to collections where the two differ so this misconception surfaces early. Having established that equal total distances define the mean, the uniqueness argument becomes intuitive — press students to state why no other point can maintain balance.
materials: Plain paper for drawing number lines

periods.activity_title: How Adding or Removing Values Shifts the Balance

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the median of a 16-value dataset; then reason about (i) one value that can be added without changing the median, (ii) two values that can be added without changing it, (iii) one value that can be removed without changing it.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine four statements about mean/median behaviour (removing a value less than median; including a value less than mean; including 4 values; including 4 values less than median) and classify each as always/sometimes/never true.

time_bands.activity: Using the balance-point model of mean established in the section, students investigate: what happens to the mean when a value larger than it is added? Smaller? Equal? Small groups test with self-chosen collections, record results, and form a conjecture before the class pools findings.

Extend the investigation to symmetric additions: students discover from section 5.1 prose that adding pairs of values equidistant around the current mean preserves balance. Groups construct at least one such pair and verify on a number line.

Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.114 ("Find the median of a 16-value dataset; then reason about (i) one value that can be added without changing the median....") — students apply parallel logic to the median as a middle-rank value and articulate the discovery.

Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.115 ("Examine four statements about mean/median behaviour... and classify each as always/sometimes/never true.") — pairs classify each statement and share a counterexample or proof sketch for those classified 'sometimes'.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is to assume that adding any even number of values will leave the mean unchanged; redirect students to the symmetry condition — the new values must be equidistant around the existing mean. Watch also for students who conflate median shift rules with mean shift rules when answering Q6.
materials: Squared or plain paper for number-line sketches

periods.activity_title: Algebraic Proof: Shifting and Scaling All Values

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This, p.107
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students explain algebraically (and using fair-share interpretation) what happens to the average when a fixed number is subtracted from every value, and then investigate what happens when every value is doubled.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: Class average height of 24 students is 150.2 cm, measured with shoes adding 1 cm; determine whether remeasurement is needed and compute the correct average height (149.2 cm) from six options.

time_bands.activity: Present the algebraic argument from section 5.1: if every value increases by a constant c, the sum increases by n×c, so the mean increases by exactly c. Walk through the symbolic steps together, naming the distributive property at each stage.

Try This, p.107 ("Students explain algebraically... what happens to the average when a fixed number is subtracted from every value, and then investigate what happens when every value is doubled.") — students write the algebra for subtraction, then for doubling, and present their reasoning step by step to a partner.

Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.113 ("Class average height of 24 students is 150.2 cm, measured with shoes adding 1 cm; determine whether remeasurement is needed and compute the correct average height....") — students apply the shift-by-constant result directly and select from the given options, justifying their choice algebraically.

Brief whole-class discussion: students state the two algebraic results in their own words — shifting all values shifts the mean by the same amount; scaling all values scales the mean by the same factor — and give a new numerical example of each.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes think that subtracting a constant might change the mean by more or less than that constant when the dataset is large; the algebraic proof directly addresses this and should be revisited if the misconception reappears. Having established the shift result, the scaling result follows by the same distributive-property logic — encourage students to write the scaling proof themselves before you confirm it.

periods.activity_title: Finding the Unknown: Mean as a Linear Equation

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Finding the Unknown (wrestlers), p.109
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given the mean weight of 10 wrestlers (39.2 kg) and 9 of the 10 weights, uses the mean formula to set up and solve a linear equation to find the missing weight (43 kg).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Finding the Unknown (coconuts), p.109
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given the average coconut harvest per tree (25.6) across 15 trees and the information that one tree's count was recorded 3 more than actual, recovers the total harvest and computes the corrected average (25.4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: The mean of 8 numbers (8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10) is 10.375; find the value of y.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: A dataset has 15 values with mean 134; find the sum of the data.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Finding the Unknown (wrestlers), p.109 ("Given the mean weight of 10 wrestlers (39.2 kg) and 9 of the 10 weights, uses the mean formula to set up and solve a linear equation to find the missing weight (43 kg).") — narrate how the total-sum relationship converts the mean formula into a solvable equation.

Students read Finding the Unknown (coconuts), p.109 ("Given the average coconut harvest per tree (25.6) across 15 trees and the information that one tree's count was recorded 3 more than actual, recovers the total harvest and computes the corrected average (25.4).") independently, then reconstruct the solution method in their own words before checking.
Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.115 ("The mean of 8 numbers (8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10) is 10.375; find the value of y.") — students set up the equation, solve, and verify by substituting back.

Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.115 ("A dataset has 15 values with mean 134; find the sum of the data.") — quick application of the sum = mean × n relationship; students articulate why no individual values are needed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently divide the known sum by the wrong count when a value is missing; emphasise that n refers to the total number of values including the unknown one. Having established both worked examples, students should see that correction problems (coconuts) are a two-step variant — total, then re-total after adjusting the erroneous entry.

periods.activity_title: Frequency Tables, Cumulative Frequencies, and Spreadsheet Formulae

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Mean and Median with Frequencies (family size), p.110
textbook_items_in_class.description: Calculates mean and median of a frequency-table dataset of family sizes for 36 students, demonstrating the weighted-sum formula for mean and the cumulative-frequency method for locating the median position.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Frequency table shows number of trials to hit a dart bull's-eye for a school competition; describe the data using minimum, maximum, mean, and median.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given 11 values including unknown p and median 29, determine which candidate values of p (10, 25, 40, 100, 29, 47, 30) are consistent with the given median.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Mean and Median with Frequencies (family size), p.110 ("Calculates mean and median of a frequency-table dataset of family sizes for 36 students, demonstrating the weighted-sum formula for mean and the cumulative-frequency method for locating the median position.") — construct the frequency table column by column, showing why value × frequency is the correct contribution to the total.

Demonstrate the cumulative-frequency column from the same worked example and locate the median position using the (n+1)/2 rule; then introduce the spreadsheet sub-topic from section 5.1 prose — cell references, range notation, and the =SUM() and =AVERAGE() formula patterns on a drawn grid on the board.

Figure it Out Q11, section 5.1 p.115 ("Frequency table shows number of trials to hit a dart bull's-eye for a school competition; describe the data using minimum, maximum, mean, and median.") — students build their own cumulative-frequency column and apply the weighted-sum formula.

Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.115 ("Given 11 values including unknown p and median 29, determine which candidate values of p....") — students reason about sorted order and the median position to screen each candidate; pairs compare their shortlists.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error in frequency tables is summing the 'value' column rather than the 'value × frequency' column; point students back to the fair-share interpretation — if five families each have size 3, they contribute 15 to the total, not 3. The spreadsheet connection is conceptual here; actual software is not required, but the formula syntax (=AVERAGE(B3:G3)) should be written on the board so students see the range notation.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for frequency table construction

periods.activity_title: Consolidated Practice on Mean, Median, and Dot Plots

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the mean of (i) first 50 natural numbers, (ii) first 50 odd numbers, (iii) first 50 multiples of 4; share observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Dot plot shows weekly cycle-riding frequency; four students rode twice. Find average, median, evaluate five validity statements about the data, and predict next week's average and median if everyone rode one extra time.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.113 ("Find the mean of (i) first 50 natural numbers, (ii) first 50 odd numbers, (iii) first 50 multiples of 4; share observations.") — students use the shift-by-constant and scale-by-constant results proved algebraically in section 5.1 to derive each answer without computing all terms.

Figure it Out Q10, section 5.1 p.115 ("Dot plot shows weekly cycle-riding frequency; four students rode twice. Find average, median, evaluate five validity statements about the data, and predict next week's average and median if everyone rode one extra time.") — students compute mean and median from the dot plot, then use the shift-by-constant result to predict next week's values without recomputing.
Students evaluate the five validity statements in Q10 individually, then compare with a partner; differences in classification are resolved by producing a counterexample or a brief argument.
Whole-class share: one pair presents their reasoning for one disputed statement; the class reaches a consensus verdict and records the correct classification.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who compute next week's mean by hand rather than applying the +1 shift result have not internalised the algebraic consequence — use this moment to reconnect the arithmetic to the proof. Watch for students who evaluate validity statements by checking a single example; push for 'always/sometimes/never' language supported by a reason, not just a case.

periods.activity_title: Reading Line Graphs: Identify Then Infer

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Line Graphs — Temperature (Kerala and Punjab), p.116–118
textbook_items_in_class.description: Demonstrates the two-step identify-then-infer process on a clustered line graph of monthly maximum temperatures (2023), identifying scale, markers, and trends; inferring Punjab's higher variability versus Kerala's near-constant tropical climate.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tabular data of average daily customers visiting vs. purchasing across days of the week; visualise on a line graph.

time_bands.activity: Introduce section 5.2's two-step framework from the prose: Step 1 — identify what the graph shows (scale, units, markers, time range); Step 2 — infer patterns and comparisons. Students state in their own words why this order matters before looking at any graph.

Line Graphs — Temperature (Kerala and Punjab), p.116–118 ("Demonstrates the two-step identify-then-infer process on a clustered line graph of monthly maximum temperatures (2023), identifying scale, markers, and trends; inferring Punjab's higher variability versus Kerala's near-constant tropical climate.") — teacher models Step 1 aloud; students then independently attempt Step 2 inferences and share.

Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.122 ("Tabular data of average daily customers visiting vs. purchasing across days of the week; visualise on a line graph.") — students convert the table to a line graph on plain paper, choosing scale and labels, then apply the two-step process to their own graph.
Pairs exchange graphs and critique each other's Step 1 completeness — did the partner label scale, units, and both series clearly? Brief oral feedback is given; students note one correction to make.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often jump straight to inferences without reading the scale carefully, leading to magnitude errors; insisting on Step 1 as a written checklist before Step 2 helps break this habit. Having established the identify-then-infer sequence on the temperature example, students carry the same two-step discipline into every subsequent graph in this section.

periods.activity_title: Multi-Series Graphs, Infographics, and Valid Inference

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Line Graphs — Space Launches, p.119–120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Applies the two-step process to a multi-series line graph of annual space-object launches (2012–2024) for USA, China, Russia, and worldwide; distinguishes valid inferences from invalid ones (e.g., cannot infer Nepal launched nothing, cannot read individual year counts precisely from the graph).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Average monthly rainfall (days) for Mangaluru, New Delhi, Port Blair, Rameswaram; plot three cities on a given line graph, fill in New Delhi data from the graph, compare rainiest and driest cities, identify rainy seasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Line graph on primary lighting source (kerosene vs electricity) in rural/urban India 1983–2023; evaluate four validity statements.

time_bands.activity: Line Graphs — Space Launches, p.119–120 ("Applies the two-step process to a multi-series line graph of annual space-object launches (2012–2024)... distinguishes valid inferences from invalid ones....") — teacher leads Step 1 identification, then students generate inferences; teacher challenges each: 'Is this valid or an overreach?' to sharpen the distinction.

Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.122 ("Average monthly rainfall (days) for Mangaluru, New Delhi, Port Blair, Rameswaram; plot three cities on a given line graph....") — students plot the three cities, use the completed graph to read off New Delhi's data, and identify rainy seasons through the two-step process.

Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.130 ("Line graph on primary lighting source (kerosene vs electricity) in rural/urban India 1983–2023; evaluate four validity statements.") — pairs classify each statement, marking which rely on reading the graph versus inferring beyond it.
Whole-class synthesis: students name one type of invalid inference they noticed across all three graph tasks and articulate a rule for distinguishing reading from over-reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error across multi-series graphs is inferring that an absent series label means zero — the space-launches example directly addresses this and should be referenced when students make similar errors on the rainfall or kerosene graphs. The choropleth infographic from section 5.2 prose (per-capita rice and wheat consumption) can be described verbally to deepen the discussion of colour-encoding versus table-reading; no separate worked example is needed.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This, p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students create their own 48-box activity strip for different days of the week, marking five activity types in 30-minute intervals, and compare their strip with an adult family member's strip.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Individual project: create activity strips for different days of the week; track eating/sleeping regularity and outdoor time; calculate average time per activity; compare with an adult's strip.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the activity-strip representation from section 5.2 prose: a 48-box colour-coded row where each box represents a 30-minute interval across one day and five activity types are distinguished by colour. Students draw a blank 48-box strip on plain paper and label the time intervals.

Teacher reads aloud the description of Manoj's Friday strip from the section prose; students decode it — counting boxes per activity and computing time in hours — then infer which of his three days features a long movie outing, using box counts as evidence.

Try This, p.125 ("Students create their own 48-box activity strip for different days of the week, marking five activity types in 30-minute intervals, and compare their strip with an adult family member's strip.") — each student fills in their own strip for today (or yesterday, recalled from memory) using five agreed activity colours, then calculates total minutes per activity.

Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.131 ("Individual project: create activity strips for different days of the week... calculate average time per activity; compare with an adult's strip.") — students begin a second strip for a different day and compute the average time per activity across both strips, completing the comparison in class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may leave boxes blank when they cannot recall exactly what they were doing; encourage an 'other' colour so every box is filled and the strip remains a complete 24-hour record. Having decoded Manoj's strips before creating their own, students internalise the reading discipline before the creative task — this sequence also means the strips start and end within this sitting and no earlier preparation is assumed.
materials: Plain paper (each student needs two sheets for strips)
At least 5 coloured pencils or crayons per student

periods.activity_title: Smooth Curves, Moonrise Patterns, and Extended Data Exploration

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This, p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students read a line graph of moonrise and moonset times over a month, identify the dates of amavasya (new moon) and purnima (full moon), and note patterns.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (births graph), section 5.2 p.123
textbook_items_in_class.description: Line graph of monthly births in India over a time period; make observations, estimate births in July 2017, identify time period captured, compare January births across 2018–2020, estimate total births in 2019.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q14, section 5.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Four line graphs show sunrise and sunset times across the year at 4 Indian locations; identify sunrise vs sunset lines, find earliest January sunrise, find location with longest day, share observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q15, section 5.2 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Line graph of moonrise and moonset times over one month; identify dates of new moon and full moon, note patterns.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the sleep-duration curve from section 5.2 prose: a line graph of average daily sleep from age 6 to 75 with 80 closely spaced data points that form a smooth curve. Students discuss why a line graph is more readable than 70 columns would be and identify the adolescence dip, mid-adulthood minimum, and post-50 rise from the description.

Try This, p.131 ("Students read a line graph of moonrise and moonset times over a month, identify the dates of amavasya (new moon) and purnima (full moon), and note patterns.") — students apply the two-step identify-then-infer process to a periodic, non-trend line graph for the first time, noticing how the two series converge and diverge across the month.

Figure it Out Q14, section 5.2 p.131 ("Four line graphs show sunrise and sunset times across the year at 4 Indian locations; identify sunrise vs sunset lines, find earliest January sunrise, find location with longest day, share observations.") — groups tackle the identification challenge (which line is sunrise?) by reasoning from the known pattern that sunrise is earlier and sunset later in summer.

Figure it Out Q3 (births graph), section 5.2 p.123 ("Line graph of monthly births in India over a time period; make observations, estimate births in July 2017, identify time period captured, compare January births across 2018–2020, estimate total births in 2019.") — students practise reading off and estimating values from a real-data graph with seasonal and multi-year structure, sharing at least one observation the graph supports and one it cannot support.

periods.teacher_notes: The sunrise/sunset identification in Q14 is a productive struggle item — students who try to read labels directly will be stuck; nudge them to reason from physical knowledge (shorter days in winter) to distinguish the two lines. Having worked through periodic graphs (moonrise/moonset) and smooth curves (sleep), students now encounter a multi-year seasonal pattern (births) — connecting these as different reasons a line graph is preferred over a bar chart consolidates the section's central idea.

items.prompt: A set of five numbers has a mean of 12. A student claims: 'If I add the number 12 to this set, the mean of the new six-number set will still be 12.' Which of the following best explains why this claim is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Adding any number to a set never changes the mean.

options.label: B
options.text: Adding the mean itself to the set leaves the balance point undisturbed, because the new value contributes no net pull in either direction.

options.label: C
options.text: The mean of the new set equals the mean of the old set plus 12, divided by 2.

options.label: D
options.text: Adding a number equal to the mean doubles the mean.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B. The original mean is 12, so the original sum is 60. Adding 12 gives a new sum of 72 and a new count of 6. New mean = 72 ÷ 6 = 12. The added value equals the existing mean, so it sits exactly at the balance point and exerts no net pull.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the balance-point model: a value placed exactly at the mean adds equal distance on neither side, leaving the mean unchanged.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student overgeneralises, believing any addition preserves the mean rather than understanding the special role of adding the mean itself.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the mean-update rule with an averaging-of-means formula, incorrectly treating the new mean as (old mean + new value) ÷ 2.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has a fundamental misconception that adding a value equal to the mean multiplies rather than preserves it.

inclusivity.support: Let the student compute the original sum (5 × 12) and the new sum after adding 12, then divide by 6 to see the mean stays the same.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: for which added value would the new mean be exactly 13? Generalise: if the original mean is m over n values, what single value v must be added to raise the mean to m + 1?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.113
exercise.description: A dot plot shows a collection with its mean of 9 but one dot is missing; mark the missing value to restore the balance.

items.prompt: A sorted dataset of 10 values has a median of 18. Priya wants to add two new values to the dataset so that the median of the 12-value dataset remains 18. She proposes adding the values 10 and 26. Will her proposal work? Justify your answer using the definition of median for an even number of values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: With 12 values the median is the average of the 6th and 7th values in sorted order. Originally the 5th and 6th values averaged to 18. Inserting 10 (below 18) and 26 (above 18) keeps the sorted list symmetric around position 18 for the new 6th and 7th values, so their average remains 18. Priya's proposal works because one value falls below and one above the existing median, preserving the central pair.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the even-n median rule: the median is the average of the two middle values; adding one value below and one above 18 keeps the new middle pair averaging to 18.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write out a concrete 10-value sorted list with median 18, insert 10 and 26, re-sort, and locate positions 6 and 7.
inclusivity.challenge: What is the range of pairs (a, b) with a < 18 < b that Priya could add and still keep the median at 18? Is there any pair with both values above 18 that also works?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.114
exercise.description: Find the median of a 16-value dataset; then reason about (i) one value that can be added without changing the median, (ii) two values that can be added without changing it, (iii) one value that can be removed without changing it.

items.prompt: A class recorded scores for six students: 72, 68, 85, 90, 77, 64. Their teacher later realised that each score was measured with a tool that added 3 extra marks to every student's score. Without computing the corrected mean from scratch, explain how the corrected mean relates to the original mean, and state the corrected mean.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Original sum = 72 + 68 + 85 + 90 + 77 + 64 = 456. Original mean = 456 ÷ 6 = 76. Because every value was inflated by 3, the corrected values are each 3 less, so the corrected sum is 456 − (6 × 3) = 438, and the corrected mean is 438 ÷ 6 = 73. Equivalently, by the constant-shift result proved algebraically in section 5.1, subtracting 3 from every value decreases the mean by exactly 3. Corrected mean = 76 − 3 = 73.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the constant-shift result: subtracting a fixed constant c from every value decreases the mean by exactly c.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first compute the original mean by hand, then ask: if I subtract 3 from each of the 6 values, how does the total change, and therefore how does the mean change?
inclusivity.challenge: Suppose the tool also multiplied each true score by 1.05 after adding 3 — what algebraic expression gives the corrected mean in terms of the measured mean?

exercise.description: Students explain algebraically (and using fair-share interpretation) what happens to the average when a fixed number is subtracted from every value, and then investigate what happens when every value is doubled.

items.prompt: The mean of seven numbers is 15. Six of the numbers are 11, 18, 9, 22, 14, and 16. Find the seventh number. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total sum = 7 × 15 = 105. Sum of known six = 11 + 18 + 9 + 22 + 14 + 16 = 90. Seventh number = 105 − 90 = 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use sum = mean × n to find the required total, then subtract the known values to isolate the unknown.

inclusivity.support: Provide the equation frame: 7 × 15 = (sum of six known numbers) + seventh number, and ask the student to fill in each part.
inclusivity.challenge: If the seventh number were instead 20, what would the new mean be? Generalise: if the seventh number is k, express the mean as a formula in k.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.115
exercise.description: The mean of 8 numbers (8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10) is 10.375; find the value of y.

items.prompt:
The table below shows the number of books read by students in a reading club and the number of students who read that many books. Calculate the mean and median number of books read. Show all working.

| Books read | Number of students |
|---|---|
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 7 |
| 4 | 5 |
| 5 | 3 |
| 6 | 1 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total students n = 4 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 20. Weighted sum = (2×4) + (3×7) + (4×5) + (5×3) + (6×1) = 8 + 21 + 20 + 15 + 6 = 70. Mean = 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5 books. For median: cumulative frequencies are 4, 11, 16, 19, 20. With 20 values the median is the average of the 10th and 11th values. The 10th value falls in the group 'books = 3' (cumulative up to 3 is 11, up to 2 is 4, so positions 5–11 are all 3). The 11th value is also in the group 'books = 3'. Median = (3 + 3) ÷ 2 = 3 books.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the weighted-sum formula (value × frequency, summed, divided by total frequency) for the mean, and cumulative frequencies to locate the median position.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to add a 'value × frequency' column to the table and total it before dividing by 20.
inclusivity.challenge: If one student who read 6 books is replaced by a student who read 2 books, how do the mean and median each change? Show algebraically.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 5.1 p.115
exercise.description: Frequency table shows number of trials to hit a dart bull's-eye for a school competition; describe the data using minimum, maximum, mean, and median.

items.prompt: The first 50 even numbers are 2, 4, 6, …, 100. Without adding them all individually, find their mean. Explain how your method relates to the algebraic result that scaling every value in a dataset by a constant scales the mean by the same constant.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first 50 natural numbers are 1, 2, …, 50. Their mean = (1 + 50) ÷ 2 = 51 ÷ 2 = 25.5. The first 50 even numbers are exactly 2 × (first 50 natural numbers). By the scaling result, mean of first 50 even numbers = 2 × 25.5 = 51. Verification: sum = 2 + 4 + … + 100 = 2(1 + 2 + … + 50) = 2 × 1275 = 2550; mean = 2550 ÷ 50 = 51. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise the even numbers as 2 × (natural numbers), apply the scaling result to multiply the known mean of the naturals by 2.

inclusivity.support: Provide the fact that the mean of the first 50 natural numbers is 25.5 and ask how multiplying every number by 2 changes the mean.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the mean of the first 50 multiples of 7. Then find the mean of the first 50 odd numbers using the shift-by-constant result, starting from the naturals.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.113
exercise.description: Find the mean of (i) first 50 natural numbers, (ii) first 50 odd numbers, (iii) first 50 multiples of 4; share observations.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper records the number of customers who enter her shop and the number who make a purchase, for each day of a week. She wants to display both series on a single line graph. State two things she must do at the identify (Step 1) stage before drawing any inference, and write one valid inference she could draw from such a graph once it is drawn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1 (identify) actions — any two of: (i) label the axes clearly (horizontal = days of the week, vertical = number of customers) with units; (ii) choose a consistent scale on the vertical axis that fits both series; (iii) use distinct markers or colours for the two series and include a legend. One valid inference: if the 'purchasing' line is consistently lower than the 'visiting' line, many visitors do not buy — the gap between the two lines on any day shows how many customers left without purchasing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-step identify-then-infer process from section 5.2: complete all scale, label, and legend decisions before drawing any conclusion.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to list what information a reader needs to understand the graph before looking at the lines (axis labels, scale, legend), then name one question the completed graph could answer.
inclusivity.challenge: What additional information would be needed to draw the inference that Sundays are the best sales day, and what distinguishes a valid inference from a speculative one?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.122
exercise.description: Tabular data of average daily customers visiting vs. purchasing across days of the week; visualise on a line graph.

items.prompt: A line graph shows average monthly rainfall (in rainy days) for four cities over a year. City W has its highest value in July (22 days) and its lowest in January (0 days). City X shows values between 8 and 15 days throughout the year with no clear peak. Identify which city has the more pronounced rainy season and explain how you used the graph's pattern — not just individual values — to reach that conclusion.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: City W has the more pronounced rainy season. The evidence is the sharp rise and fall of its line — values climb steeply from near zero in winter months to 22 days in July, then drop steeply again. This spike pattern, where the line forms a clear peak, indicates a concentrated rainy season. City X's line stays relatively flat throughout the year, indicating rainfall is spread across all months with no distinct rainy season. The inference rests on the shape of the line (pattern), not on reading any single month's value.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-step identify-then-infer method: read the shape and range of each city's line, then infer seasonal concentration from the steepness of rise and fall.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to sketch a rough shape of each city's line (spiky vs flat) and then say which shape suggests a concentrated rainy season.
inclusivity.challenge: How would you quantify which city has the more variable rainfall — what numerical measure from section 5.1 could you compute from the monthly values, and what would a larger value indicate?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.122
exercise.description: Average monthly rainfall (days) for Mangaluru, New Delhi, Port Blair, Rameswaram; plot three cities on a given line graph, fill in New Delhi data from the graph, compare rainiest and driest cities, identify rainy seasons.

items.prompt: Riya creates a 48-box activity strip for a Saturday. She uses five colours: Sleep (blue), Study (green), Outdoor play (yellow), Screen time (red), and Other (grey). She counts 16 blue boxes, 4 green boxes, 10 yellow boxes, 8 red boxes, and 10 grey boxes. Calculate the average time Riya spent on each activity per day (in hours), and state which two activities together account for exactly half of her day.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each box = 30 minutes = 0.5 hours. Sleep: 16 × 0.5 = 8 h. Study: 4 × 0.5 = 2 h. Outdoor play: 10 × 0.5 = 5 h. Screen time: 8 × 0.5 = 4 h. Other: 10 × 0.5 = 5 h. Total = 8 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 5 = 24 h ✓. Half the day = 12 h. Sleep (8 h) + Outdoor play (5 h) = 13 h — no. Sleep (8 h) + Screen time (4 h) = 12 h ✓. So Sleep and Screen time together account for exactly half the day.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert box counts to hours (each box = 0.5 h), compute each activity's total, then find the pair summing to 12 h.

inclusivity.support: Provide the conversion: 1 box = 30 minutes = 0.5 hours, and ask the student to multiply each box count by 0.5 to get hours before looking for the pair.
inclusivity.challenge: If Riya wants her average Study time to double next Saturday without changing her Sleep time, which other activity or activities could she reduce, and by how many boxes?

exercise.description: Students create their own 48-box activity strip for different days of the week, marking five activity types in 30-minute intervals, and compare their strip with an adult family member's strip.

items.prompt: A line graph shows moonrise times over 30 days. For the first 15 days the moonrise time gets later and later each night (the line slopes upward). For the next 15 days the moonrise time gets earlier and earlier each night (the line slopes downward). On which day does the line reach its highest point, and what does that day most likely represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Day 1; it represents the new moon (amavasya) because moonrise is earliest at the start of the lunar cycle.

options.label: B
options.text: Day 15; it represents the full moon (purnima) because the moon rises latest near the middle of the lunar cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: Day 30; it represents the new moon (amavasya) because the cycle completes at the end of the month.

options.label: D
options.text: Day 15; it represents the new moon (amavasya) because the moon is invisible at the peak of the graph.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B. The peak (Day 15) is when moonrise is latest in the night. The full moon (purnima) rises near sunset and sets near sunrise — it is visible all night. Near the new moon (amavasya) the moon rises close to sunrise and is barely visible. The graph pattern — rising then falling moonrise times — places purnima at the peak, consistent with section 5.2 prose.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the peak of the line graph and connect it to the physical meaning described in section 5.2: purnima corresponds to the latest moonrise in the lunar month.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student misidentifies the earliest moonrise (start of graph) as the key lunar event, confusing amavasya with the graph's minimum rather than its maximum.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student locates the correct lunar event (new moon at cycle end) but confuses the end of the 30-day graph with the peak, misreading graph direction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly identifies Day 15 as the peak but incorrectly associates the latest moonrise with the new moon rather than the full moon.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that the graph's highest point means moonrise happens latest that night, then ask: which phase of the moon is visible all night long?
inclusivity.challenge: Sketch what the moonset-time graph would look like over the same 30 days, and identify the day when moonrise and moonset times are closest together.

exercise.description: Students read a line graph of moonrise and moonset times over a month, identify the dates of amavasya (new moon) and purnima (full moon), and note patterns.
